title: Binary Trees: Inorder Traversal (DFS)
oneLiner: Left subtree, then this node, then right subtree -- on a BST, that order comes out sorted for free.
keyTakeaway: Inorder traversal (left, node, right) is one of three classic depth-first orders (preorder is node-left-right, postorder is left-right-node) -- all three are the same "go as deep as possible before backtracking (going back up to try the next branch)" DFS (depth-first search) shape, just differing in WHEN you visit the current node relative to its children. On a binary SEARCH tree specifically, inorder always produces values in fully sorted order -- not a coincidence, it's a direct consequence of the BST invariant (left < node <= right, with equal values going right) applied recursively at every level.
explanation: Depth-first traversal means fully exploring one subtree before moving to the next, rather than sweeping across a level at a time (that's breadth-first instead). Inorder specifically means: recursively traverse the whole left subtree first, then visit the current node, then recursively traverse the whole right subtree. On a plain binary tree that's just one particular visiting order among several valid ones -- but on a BST, it's guaranteed to produce every value in ascending sorted order, because at every single node, the entire left subtree is smaller and the entire right subtree is bigger or equal, all the way down. Watch out for the base case: an empty subtree (a null child) contributes nothing and returns immediately -- forgetting that check, or visiting the current node before fully finishing the left subtree, are the two most common ways to get the order wrong.

recognitionSignals: You need to visit every node of a tree, and the RELATIVE order of visiting matters (not just "touch everything").
The problem is naturally recursive: "the answer for this tree = something combined with the answer for its left subtree and its right subtree."
gotchas: Forgetting the null-child base case turns the recursion into a crash (NullReferenceException / AttributeError on None) instead of just contributing nothing.
Visiting the node before recursing left (that's preorder, not inorder) is the single most common mix-up between the three DFS orders.
On a tree that ISN'T a BST, inorder traversal still runs fine -- it just doesn't come out sorted. The sorted guarantee is a BST-specific consequence, not a property of inorder traversal itself.
confusableWith: Binary Search Trees: Insert (this track) builds the shape inorder traversal reads back out -- insertion and traversal are opposite directions through the same invariant.

Binary Trees: Level-Order Traversal (BFS) visits nodes a whole depth-level at a time using a queue, rather than fully diving into one subtree first with recursion -- the tell is whether "depth" or "level" is what the problem cares about.

complexity.note: Every node is visited exactly once; the recursion stack is as deep as the tree is tall (O(log n) balanced, O(n) worst), not counting the output list.
